why: within 3 days of Copom decision (3-4 Nov) (2026-11-04)

questions.base_rate_used: Scenario page base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns with a stable outlook going in (0%, and 0% as a lower bound on the wider count). S&P usually moves the outlook to negative before it cuts, so I start near zero and allow a small tail for an off-pattern cut.

factors.text: The reference class is clean on this point. S&P has not cut any of these six EU sovereigns straight from a stable outlook since 2014. The normal path is an outlook change first, and an outlook change alone resolves NO. This is the main reason I sit well below the market.

The fiscal and political backdrop is getting worse, which gives S&P cover to act. HCFP calls the 1.0% growth forecast optimistic and sees debt rising toward about 122%. Budget adoption by 31 December is close to a coin flip (50.5% and 49%). Marine Le Pen is priced at 41.1% to win in 2027. The OAT-Bund spread widened from 81.5bp to 96.7bp on the monthly series. This mostly argues for a negative outlook, but it keeps a direct cut possible.

Where the crowd may share an error: the 26.5% Polymarket price trades on thin volume (7345). The 31% Kalshi contract covers any agency through year-end, so it is wider than this question. Both seem to treat a bad fiscal story as if it meant an S&P cut on 27 Nov, and skip the outlook-first habit. The spread series is a degraded monthly average, and no gauge here is tested as a lead on rating actions.

questions.what_would_change_view: Any of these before 27 Nov would push me up toward the market: the government falls on a censure motion, PLF 2027 is rejected at first reading so a special law becomes the base case, or the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate. A confirmation that S&P's current outlook is already negative, not stable, would also break the reference class. A quiet first reading with the revenue part passed would push me toward affirm_stable.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The 'stable outlook going in' premise could be wrong, or S&P could decide that political paralysis before the 2027 election justifies an off-pattern cut. In either case the 0% reference class does not apply and the market's roughly one-in-four is closer to right.
questions.title: S&P review of France, 27 Nov 2026

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. I give more weight to the subset since France lost its majority in 2022. The page shows that subset separately but does not quote it. Its branch notes say the 2024 and 2025 cycles both ended with a special law. The most relevant starting point is therefore roughly a coin flip for a minority government, well below 90.5%.

factors.text: Structural: a minority government since the 2024 dissolution. The last two budget cycles both missed 31 December and ended with a special law, the 2024 and 2025 pattern noted on the scenario page. The full-sample base rate of 90.5% mostly comes from years with a majority.

This budget is politically harder than usual. It has about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions and of the civil-service pay index. It lands just before the spring 2027 presidential race, in which Le Pen has launched her campaign and is priced at 41.1%. Opposition parties gain little from letting it pass, and a 49.3 invites a censure vote.

The government has tools to force it through. Kalshi prices use of Article 49.3 on the budget in 2026 at 66%. The Article 47 deadline of 10 December also opens a never-used ordinance route. This keeps the chance of adoption well above zero, provided the government survives.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if PS or LR publicly commit not to censure a 49.3 text, or if a joint committee agreement is reached in mid-December. I would move down if a censure motion gathers PS votes, if the revenue part fails at first reading in November, or if the government signals a special law as in 2024 and 2025.
questions.most_likely_wrong: Prediction markets at 50.5% and 49% may be right. The government may have secured a quiet non-censure deal, like the one that eventually passed the 2026 budget, and simply land it before Christmas this time, given the reputational cost of a third consecutive special law. My pre-election pessimism could then be overdone. The market signals themselves carry little tested evidence, and the official-optimism gauge is untested.
questions.title: France 2027 budget and the Article 47 deadline

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed probability for an RN win. Its reference class says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 presidential run-offs, with an RMS poll error of 5.78 pp. That only helps once final polls exist, and the snapshot holds no polls six months out. As a last resort I start from market prices: on Polymarket, Le Pen at 41.1% plus Bardella at 1.7%; on Kalshi, Le Pen at 45% plus Bardella at 1.4%. Together that puts the RN candidate in the low-to-mid 40s.

factors.text: Markets price the RN candidate highest among single candidates. Le Pen has formally launched her campaign, and headlines are framing the race as hers to lose. That keeps the starting point near the market level. Note that the market splits RN odds between Le Pen and Bardella as though her ineligibility case were mostly settled; the question counts either name, so that split does not change the YES side.

The centre-right side is split across Lisnard at 19.6%, Philippe at 14.5%, Lagarde at 4.2% and others, and together they are close to the RN total. A run-off is usually a two-way race in which non-RN voters consolidate, and the signposts say that consolidation (withdrawals, sponsorship totals in March 2027) has not happened yet. I shade slightly below the market because fragmented anti-RN odds tend to understate the eventual run-off opponent.

The crowd's main gauge carries little evidential weight. The poll-versus-prediction-market gap is badged tested_no_lead, and prediction-market series in general are tested_no_lead. These markets have high volume but are untested as forecasters this far out. Fiscal strain could still feed the anti-incumbent vote: HCFP expects debt to rise toward about 122% of GDP and sees the 2029 deficit target as very unlikely to be met.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if second-round polls against the leading centre-right candidate show RN ahead by more than the 5.78 pp historical poll error, or if the centre-right stays split into March 2027. I would move down if one centre-right candidate consolidates (the others withdraw) and run-off polls show RN behind. A ruling that keeps Le Pen off the ballot would matter only if Bardella polled weaker than her.
questions.most_likely_wrong: I may be underrating RN. The old pattern of anti-RN voters uniting in the run-off may have weakened enough, under fiscal austerity and a polarised climate, that the market's low-to-mid 40s is too low rather than too high.
questions.title: France 2027 presidential election

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. I start from a judgement reference class instead. Brazil cut self-set targets in July 2015 and April 2024, but in both cases the cut came with or after mid-year reviews or the April budget-guidelines bill, not in the first quarter. Re-elected or new governments usually prefer workarounds to formal cuts in the first months. That points to a starting point of about two in three that the formal target and rule survive to 31 March.

factors.text: Independent estimates are far below the 0.5% target. The IFI sees an effective 2027 surplus of only 0.1% of GDP, and a potential deficit of 1.0%, with about R$40 billion unbudgeted. The Focus median is -0.3%, below even the lower tolerance bound. That builds pressure to rewrite the target. But the 'official optimism gap' gauge is untested, so this is a direction, not a timing signal.

The window is short and the government's own numbers say the target is met: the budget bill counts a surplus of 0.6% of GDP against the 0.5% target. The new term starts 5 January. The first 2027 bimonthly report (around 22 March) is built on budget-time assumptions, so it is more likely to freeze spending or lean on deductions than to propose a cut before 31 March. That favours the 'kept on paper' branch, which still resolves YES.

Markets have repriced sharply for fiscal loosening since Lula's run-off win: the DI Jan-29 proxy rose 212bp and the real fell 7.61% in a week. That makes a formal loosening plausible. It also raises the cost of one, which argues for quiet workarounds over a bill. The CBS transition adds a R$33.8 billion payment that counts toward the target, one more source of pressure.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would lower P(yes) if ministers publicly question the 0.5% target, if a PLN or PLP is drafted in December or January, if the December budget vote adds new carve-outs written into LC 200 itself, or if the new finance minister talks of 'revising' the framework. I would raise it if the first finance minister named commits to the framework and the March report announces a large spending freeze.
questions.most_likely_wrong: A newly re-elected Lula moves fast: in 2023 his government replaced the spending ceiling within months. Facing an IFI estimate of a 1.0% deficit, the government could send a bill early in 2027, before the April budget-guidelines cycle, to reset the 2027 target. That would collapse the 'kept on paper' branch, which carries most of my YES.
questions.title: Brazil 2027: fiscal-framework credibility

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page's base rate (final-poll leader won 3 of 3 Mexican midterms, 2009, 2015 and 2021; RMS poll error 4.12 pp) is about who comes first, not about a two-thirds majority. So there is no computed base rate for this exact question. I start from the same three-midterm reference class, read for supermajority retention. The only case described as starting from a governing supermajority is 2021, when the coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. That points to a starting point below even odds, which I take as roughly 35-40%.

factors.text: Midterm precedent: in 2021 the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. A two-thirds bloc needs a high vote share (the page's signpost is above 55%) plus favourable over-representation rulings, and both are harder to repeat in a midterm than in a presidential year.

Morena remains dominant. Polymarket gives it 87.4% to win the most seats and Kalshi 86.0%, and in 2024 Sheinbaum won by 33pp, well beyond her 17pp poll lead. These markets only price coming first, which every branch except a large loss satisfies, so they say little about two-thirds.

The economic backdrop is soft for a ruling party heading into a midterm. The 2026 growth median is 1.4%, the 2027 package consolidates less (RFSP deficit 3.9%) and depends on record tax collection and tight spending, and US trade friction continues ahead of the July 2027 USMCA review.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if early-2027 polls put the coalition's combined vote above 55%, or if the INE confirms the 2024 reading of the coalition over-representation rules. I would move down if coalition polls fall into the 45-55% band or the opposition forms PAN-PRI or MC alliances in key districts. Candidate registration in January 2027 is the first hard signpost.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The midterm-loss pattern may not apply: Sheinbaum's popularity and a fragmented opposition could repeat 2024, when the result beat the polls by a wide margin. Over-representation rulings could also convert a vote share near 55% into two-thirds of seats. Separately, the crowd may be making the opposite mistake to mine: the only liquid markets price 'most seats', so a headline near 87% can be misread as confidence in a supermajority. Prediction-market signals are tested_no_lead and pollster house effects are untested, so neither deserves much weight.
questions.title: Mexico midterms, 6 Jun 2027

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. As a last resort I start from market prices on the earlier, 2026 version of the question: Kalshi puts a formal 16-year extension in 2026 at 12.0% and Polymarket puts USMCA extended in 2026 at 8.5%. Our question runs to 1 July 2027, so the window is longer and the starting point sits slightly higher, around 10-15%.

factors.text: The 2026 review is ending without a 16-year extension. The markets for an extension this year are low (12.0% and 8.5%). Under art. 34.7, failing to extend means annual joint reviews, with the next on 1 July 2027. Annual reviews are the default path, and they give Washington yearly leverage it has little reason to give up. The extra months to July 2027 raise the odds only modestly above the 2026 prices.

Kalshi prices a US withdrawal notice in 2026 at 13.0%, at or above the extension odds. A Trilateral revised deal in 2026 is priced at 24.0% and a formal amendment at 11.0%. The crowd sees renegotiation and threats as more likely than a clean renewal. A written confirmation from all three parties needs every capital to agree at once, and Canada's withdrawal notice is priced at 5.0%, so the US is not the only party in play.

On 2 November USTR did two things at once. It sought Mexico's review of alleged denial of workers' rights at Madobox, and it announced a memorandum of understanding at Industrias Tecnos. The labour-enforcement channel is working and disputes are being settled one plant at a time. That is a mild sign a cooperative path still exists, which keeps the YES case alive rather than near zero. The 2027 public consultation, a placeholder dated 1 February 2027, is the formal step where an extension recommendation could appear.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if USTR's 2027 consultation report recommends extension, or if US tariffs on Mexican goods are cut below 10% (the scenario's signposts). A joint statement after the next US-Mexico bilateral round, currently a placeholder for 30 November, would also count. I would move down if US officials describe withdrawal as leverage, a Federal Register notice appears, or the US proposes separate bilateral texts. Today's US midterm result matters too, as it shapes how much the administration wants a trade win versus continued leverage.
questions.most_likely_wrong: An administration that prizes deals could trade a headline 16-year extension for Mexican and Canadian concessions before July 2027, timed as a political win. Low-volume prediction markets (volumes in the low thousands) would not anticipate that kind of unscheduled announcement. The pm. and ks. signals are badged tested_no_lead, so the market starting point itself deserves little weight.
questions.title: USMCA annual review, 1 Jul 2027

why_it_matters.text: The long end of Brazil's curve has repriced for fiscal risk, not for the central bank. Over the week the DI Jan-29 proxy rose from 12.83% to 14.95% and the Jan-31 proxy from 12.88% to 15.36%. The Jan-27 proxy, which mostly tracks the next few Copom meetings, only went from 13.44% to 13.54%. The longest fixed-rate Tesouro bond is at 15.29% and the longest IPCA+ real yield at 7.48%. With the Selic unchanged at 13.75%, investors are demanding a much larger premium to lend long to the incoming Lula term. They are not forecasting higher policy rates soon. These are degraded proxies (Tesouro LTN yields, not B3 DI swaps).

The real lost 7.61% in a week: USD/BRL PTAX went from 5.0377 to 5.4212. This followed the 25 Oct run-off, where Lula beat odds that gave Flávio Bolsonaro 80% and the 10-year rose 255bp on day 1. em-macro's hold-out tested whether currencies bounce back after elections, and they did not. Election currency moves continued rather than reversed, and the rule of betting against the day-1 move lost money, including on Brazil's 2022 run-off. History therefore gives no reason to expect a quick rebound in the real.

The fiscal gap is the core of the repricing. The 2027 budget bill claims a surplus counted for the target of 0.6% of GDP against the 0.5% target. The IFI sees an effective surplus of only 0.1% of GDP and says the target holds only if about R$35.7 billion of discretionary spending is frozen. It also warns of a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% and about R$40 billion of unbudgeted revenue. The Focus median for 2027 is -0.3%. Every independent estimate sits below the official number, so bonds will react to any sign of whether the gap is closed by freezes, by exclusions, or by changing the target.

Survey and market expectations for this week's Copom disagree. The Focus median for the next Selic, collected on 23 Oct before the run-off, was 13.5%, which implies a 25bp cut. Polymarket now gives a 25bp cut only 13.5%. em-macro found that Focus dispersion helps predict misses against the survey median in Brazil (a tested_leads badge). In-sample, the real gained about 0.016% per bp of hawkish surprise on day 1. Out of sample, though, rate-surprise effects add almost nothing. Whichever way Copom goes, one side of expectations will be wrong. The effect on the currency is likely modest compared with the fiscal story.

em-macro's own valuation signals are of little use here. For the real, its currency mispricing measure did worse than assuming no change out of sample (RMSE ratio 1.09–1.29). Its spread mispricing measure was at best 1–3% better than no change, which is not significant. A claim that BRL or long yields have 'overshot fair value' therefore has no tested support.

watch.what_to_watch: First, hold or cut. A hold at 13.75% matches the prediction market but not the pre-run-off Focus median of 13.5%; a cut would be the reverse. Second, whether the statement cites the weaker real, the fiscal outlook or higher inflation expectations as reasons to pause. A dovish cut into a falling currency is the outcome most likely to push the real lower.

This is the first Focus survey that fully reflects the run-off and the Copom decision. Watch whether the 2026 year-end Selic median (13.25%) and the 2027 median (11.75%) move up, whether 2027 IPCA inflation (4.34%) rises with the weaker real, and whether the 2027 primary balance median (-0.3%) slips toward the IFI's -1.0%.

Whether the spread of 2027 Selic forecasts (now 9.0% to 14.0%) widens further. Also whether the 2027 primary-balance range (-0.9% to 0.5%) shifts down as forecasters digest the transition team's fiscal signals.

Whether the government freezes additional discretionary spending to keep 2026 on track, or revises revenue down. A large freeze would show the framework is being enforced (the 'credible' branch). Using deductions or one-offs instead would point to 'kept on paper' (the 'kept_exclusions' branch). Compare the report with the IFI's expected 2026 deficit of 0.5% of GDP.

Whether forecasters accept the bimonthly report's fiscal numbers: does the 2026 primary median (-0.48%) improve or worsen? Also whether year-end exchange-rate and inflation forecasts keep rising after the PTAX move to 5.4212.

This is the last survey before the swap contracts the BCB is rolling over mature on 1 Dec, and before the December Copom. Check whether the 2026 year-end Selic median still implies a December cut, and whether the 2027 primary median has moved toward or away from the 0.5% target.

risks.text: A formal change to the 2027 target or to LC 200/2023 sent by the new administration. The scenario page's analog for a loosening (the November 2024 package) moved the DI Jan-29 proxy up 112bp and USD/BRL up 4.39% in three trading days, on top of the moves already seen.

A Copom cut while the real is falling and long yields are rising. That would read as the central bank putting growth ahead of the currency. This risk is sharper because the Focus median taken before the run-off expected a cut while the prediction market does not.

Political contestation. Headlines say Bolsonaro refuses to accept the result. Markets put small but rising odds on Moraes leaving the Supreme Court (6.2% on Polymarket, 10.0% before 2027 on Kalshi) and 2.5% on the election being annulled. Any escalation would add political risk to the fiscal risk.

The currency move keeps going. In em-macro's hold-out, election currency moves continued rather than reversed, so positioning for a rebound has a poor record. The BCB's FX swap auctions are announced only as rollovers of the 1 Dec contracts. Without new hedging supply from the BCB, a continued selloff could run further.
The US backdrop. The US 10-year yield is 4.94% and the midterms are today. A jump in US yields or the dollar would widen Brazil's long premium further, whatever happens domestically.

consensus.view: Surveys still describe an easing cycle and moderate fiscal slippage. Focus (23 Oct, before the run-off) expected a cut to 13.5% at this Copom, a Selic of 13.25% at end-2026 and 11.75% at end-2027, and a 2027 primary balance of -0.3% of GDP. The government's budget bill says the 0.5% target will be met at 0.6%. The IFI expects 0.1% effective, and a potential 1.0% deficit. Market prices have moved away from the surveys. Polymarket gives a November cut only 13.5%, Kalshi has 68.0% on exactly 5 cuts in 2026, and the long end and the real have repriced sharply (DI Jan-31 proxy 15.36%, PTAX 5.4212). The market is pricing a large fiscal-risk premium on the incoming term; the surveys have not yet caught up.

BR.might_be_wrong: The shared assumption, across both the falling market and the forecasters who expect slippage, is that a Lula fourth term means the framework will be loosened. The more likely path may be the familiar Brazilian compromise: the 0.5% target kept on paper, met through deductions, exclusions and spending freezes. That counts as keeping the framework on the scenario page, and it is how the budget bill already reaches its 0.6% figure. If so, the long end may be pricing an outright target cut that never arrives formally. The yields are then too high for the formal outcome, even though the real fiscal position is as weak as the IFI says. The opposite error is also possible. Focus forecasts dated 23 Oct still embed a cut path, and Focus Selic forecasts are tested_no_lead as a signal. The survey 'consensus' may simply be stale rather than a genuine view, so it should not be read as evidence the market has overreacted. Positioning (leveraged funds at the 67.3 percentile) is tested_no_lead and says nothing either way.

why_it_matters.text: Banxico is widely expected to hold at 6.5% on 5 November. em-macro finds that holds are non-events for currencies, with a day-1 move of -0.02%. It also finds that rate-surprise regressions add almost nothing out of sample, with a pooled FX correlation of 0.18. So the peso's near-term direction is more likely to come from trade news and global risk than from this decision.

Mexico's 10-year yield is the clearest rate-surprise responder in em-macro's fit sample, at +0.50bp per bp of surprise (t=6.1). A surprise 25bp cut, which markets price at 13.6%, would therefore reach the Mbono curve more than the peso. The 10-year Mbono auction yield is 9.25%, down 10bp. The caveat is that this bond relationship was not retested cleanly out of sample, and the rate regressions weakened after 2022.

The 2027 package cuts the broad deficit (RFSP) only from 4.1% to 3.9% of GDP. México Evalúa says that is still above the 2.5% the IMF recommends and not enough to stabilise debt. The plan also leans on a 69.2% cut in Pemex support, to 81.1 billion pesos, while Pemex lost 28 billion pesos in the first half of 2026. Index eligibility depends on the middle of the three agency ratings, so fiscal slippage is the slow-moving risk for Mbonos.

The peso has decoupled from Brazil. USD/BRL rose 7.61% over the week after the run-off, while USD/MXN rose only 0.69% to 18.7962. Leveraged funds hold a large net long peso position: 68,335 contracts, 24.5% of open interest, at the 79.5 percentile. That positioning gauge is badged tested_no_lead, so it does not predict direction. It does mean many holders could sell at once if a shock arrives.

USTR opened a labour-rights case at Madobox and signed a memorandum of understanding at Industrias Tecnos on 2 November. This shows the USMCA enforcement channel is active ahead of the July 2027 review. The 2016 analog for a likely withdrawal moved USD/MXN by 13.74% in 3 days, which makes trade the peso's largest tail risk.

No model in em-macro gives an edge here. For Mexico, the spread-mispricing signal is at best 0.99 against a no-change forecast and not significant, and the currency-mispricing signal is 0.95–0.99. Treat 'cheap' or 'rich' valuation arguments for Mbonos or the peso with caution.

watch.what_to_watch: Markets price a hold at 87.0% and a 25bp cut at 13.6%, and the survey median for the Q4 policy rate is 6.5%. A hold should be a non-event. If Banxico cuts, watch whether long Mbono yields fall more than the peso weakens, as the fit-sample bond sensitivity implies. In either case, read the statement for guidance on the 17 December meeting. TIIE 28-day at 6.8061% sits above the 6.5% target, so check that money-market rates are not drifting further.

Check whether the Chamber keeps the Pemex capital contribution at 81.1 billion pesos, or adds spending that pushes the RFSP above the 3.9% of GDP planned for 2027. Morena's majority makes approval itself likely. What matters is whether the numbers drift. KBRA's BBB stable affirmation came before this vote, so a looser final budget would weigh on agency views later.
watch.event: Chamber of Deputies deadline to approve the 2027 spending budget (PEF)

watch.what_to_watch: This date is a placeholder, so first watch whether a round is actually announced. Watch for more labour-rights cases like Madobox, for any withdrawal language from US officials, and for tariff announcements outside the calendar. Kalshi prices a US withdrawal notice in 2026 at 13.0% and a formal 16-year extension at 12.0%, with under two months of 2026 left.
watch.event: USMCA: US-Mexico bilateral round (next round not announced)

watch.what_to_watch: The survey figures in this brief date from 1 September, so this release refreshes stale consensus. Watch whether the 2026 inflation median of 3.87% keeps falling, which would make room for cuts. Watch whether the 2027 growth median of 1.8% slips toward the low end of the package's 1.5% to 2.5% range. And watch whether the 2027 public-sector balance median of -3.7% worsens after the budget vote.

risks.text: Trade shock off the calendar: a US withdrawal notice, tariff move or a broadened labour case could hit the peso hard. The 2016 analog moved USD/MXN by 13.74%, and there is no historical base rate for this review.

Fiscal slippage and Pemex: the 2025 broad deficit ended at 4.8% against a planned 3.9%. If growth misses, or Pemex needs more than 81.1 billion pesos, the 2027 path slips and ratings pressure returns. Index eligibility depends on the middle rating.

Crowded long peso positioning meeting emerging-market contagion: leveraged funds are at the 79.5 percentile while the Brazilian real just fell 7.61% in a week. Positioning does not predict direction (tested_no_lead), but it can amplify a sell-off once one starts.
US backdrop: today's US midterms and the 9 December FOMC could move the dollar and the US 10-year yield, now at 4.94%. Mbono yields and the peso carry trade both depend on those.

Supermajority risk at the June 2027 midterms is beyond 30 days but builds through candidate registration in January. In 2024, MXN fell 3.5% on day 1 and 7.2% by day 5 on fears of a Morena supermajority, not on a poll miss.

consensus.view: Consensus sees Mexico as a stable, slow-moving carry story. Banxico is expected on hold: no change at 87.0%, and the survey median for the Q4 2026 rate is 6.5%. Inflation is easing, with the 2026 median at 3.87%, down 0.33. Growth is modest at 1.4% for 2026, up 0.3, and 1.8% for 2027. The survey expects a 2027 public-sector balance of -3.7% of GDP. KBRA has just affirmed BBB with a stable outlook. On trade, markets see neither a 2026 extension (8.5% on Polymarket, 12.0% on Kalshi) nor a withdrawal notice (13.0%) as likely. Morena is seen winning the most seats in 2027 at 87.4%. Leveraged funds are long the peso at the 79.5 percentile.

MX.might_be_wrong: The shared error is probably treating the absence of scheduled shocks as the absence of risk. Every input in the consensus is a scheduled-calendar view: survey medians that are two months old, a hold priced at 87.0%, and KBRA's stable outlook. Mexico's big moves in em-macro came from things those tools miss. The 2024 sell-off was about a congressional supermajority that a two-candidate poll margin could not capture. US trade decisions arrive outside any calendar. The 'most seats' market at 87.4% says nothing about the two-thirds threshold that actually matters. The fiscal consensus may also share the government's optimism: the 2025 deficit came in at 4.8% against 3.9% planned. The gauge that would measure that official optimism gap is untested, so neither side has evidence it is calibrated. Finally, the peso held up while the real collapsed, and funds are heavily long. That is consistent with a market that has priced Mexico as the safe emerging-market carry trade and could reprice quickly on a single USTR headline. The positioning badge, though, says this crowding is not by itself a timing signal.

why_it_matters.text: The French 10-year spread over Germany widened sharply before the latest budget and rating news. The monthly average rose from 81.5bp in August to 96.7bp in September, and the French 10-year averaged 4.44% against 4.0%. The Bund was 3.38% on 2026-10-30. These are ECB monthly averages that can be up to five weeks old, so any October or November move is not yet visible. The series is also untested as a signal.

The 2027 budget is the main driver of the spread. The bills carry about 54 billion euros of consolidation and aim to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5.0% in 2027. The fiscal watchdog (HCFP) calls the 1.0% growth assumption optimistic. It says the plan works only if every measure passes, and it sees debt rising toward about 122% of GDP. A minority government must pass all of this, likely through Article 49.3, which invites a censure vote.

S&P reviews France on 27 November. The scenario page's own guesses for the spread are about -2bp for a plain affirmation, +4bp for a move to a negative outlook, and about 12.3bp (range 9.69 to 14.92) for a cut to A. A one-notch S&P cut is unlikely to trigger forced selling, because France would still keep a AA-category rating: Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October. That Moody's rating is the one reserve managers' thresholds hinge on.

The 2027 presidential race is already a bond story. Polymarket gives Marine Le Pen 41.1% and Kalshi 45%. The closest analog is the June 2024 dissolution, when an RN majority became possible: the spread widened about 17bp in monthly averages. That pressure can build long before the April 2027 vote.

France has no currency of its own, so French stress shows up in the spread to Germany rather than in the euro. EUR/USD was 1.1199 on 2026-10-23, down only 0.28% on the week (an untested series). The ECB's backstop (TPI) is conditional on fiscal compliance, so a failed budget weakens the safety net for French bonds more than it moves the euro.

watch.what_to_watch: Whether S&P keeps France at A+ and, more likely to matter, whether it changes the outlook. Since 2014, S&P has made 0 downgrades in 36 recorded actions on EU sovereigns that went in with a stable outlook. An outlook change would resolve the 'downgrade' markets NO but could still widen the spread. Before the date, watch three things: whether a censure motion succeeds before 27 November, whether the National Assembly passes the revenue part of PLF 2027 at first reading, and whether the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate above 5.4%. Agencies usually publish after the Friday close, so the market reaction comes the following Monday. Our monthly spread series will not show it until the December average is published.
watch.event: Standard & Poor's sovereign rating review: France

risks.text: The government falls on a censure motion over the budget. Kalshi puts use of Article 49.3 in 2026 at 66%, and each use invites a censure vote. When the Barnier government fell in December 2024, the monthly spread rose 4.7bp, which understates the daily move. The modelled effect of losing seat share is 19.08bp (range 9.0 to 29.16).

Ratings pile up rather than arriving singly. S&P reviews on 27 November and KBRA on 11 December, while Moody's Aa3 already carries a negative outlook. A further step by Moody's would threaten France's last AA-category rating, which matters for some reserve managers.

Growth and the deficit could slip. The government assumes 1.0% growth in 2027, against a consensus of 0.81%. The HCFP says downside risks dominate and that the 2029 target of a deficit below 3% is very unlikely to be met.

Election risk could be priced early. Le Pen is at 41.1% on Polymarket and has launched her campaign, and the 2024 RN analog widened the spread about 17bp. The modelled effect of a more populist government is 12.44bp, but its range includes zero.

We cannot see or forecast this market well. The spread data are monthly and lag by weeks. The em-macro spread-mispricing model did far worse than 'no change' for France (error ratio 1.59 at 3 months): it kept expecting the spread to narrow while it widened through 2024–26.

consensus.view: The three official forecasters (IMF, OECD and European Commission) put France's deficit at 5.11% of GDP in 2026 and 5.2% in 2027, slightly worse than the government's 5.0% path for 2027. They put 2027 growth at 0.81%, below the budget's 1.0%. Prediction markets treat the budget as a coin flip: 50.5% on Polymarket and 49% on Kalshi for promulgation by 31 December. That compares with 19 of 21 past budgets promulgated on time, although the special laws of 2024 and 2025 show how the minority era differs. Kalshi gives 66% to Article 49.3. Markets price a downgrade by Moody's or S&P by 30 November at 26.5%, and any agency in 2026 at 31%. Le Pen is at 41.1%. The bond market had already pushed the spread to 96.7bp by September.

FR.might_be_wrong: The crowd may be making two linked errors. First, the 26.5% price on a downgrade looks high: S&P has made 0 downgrades in 36 recorded actions on EU sovereigns going in with a stable outlook since 2014. The likelier bad outcome is an outlook change to negative, which those markets resolve NO. A NO could be misread as relief even if the spread widens a little. Second, forecasters and markets may share the government's assumption that the budget's measures will pass. The three official forecasters sit only a few tenths away from the government's numbers, and the 'official optimism gap' gauge is untested. The real tail is therefore a censure-driven special law and a further slide in growth, not the S&P date itself. Treat all of these market prices with caution: the evidence badges mark prediction markets as tested_no_lead and the French spread series as untested. History also argues against betting on a reversal. Models that called the French spread too wide failed out of sample, so 'it has widened enough' is as risky a consensus as 'the downgrade is coming'.

why_it_matters.text: Gold fell 3.06% over the week to 3949.8 even though its usual supports moved its way. The US 10-year real yield (the inflation-adjusted return on Treasuries, gold's main rival) fell 6bp to 2.60%. The broad dollar rose only 0.28%. So last week's drop was not a rates-or-dollar story. The clearest match is the Geopolitical Risk index, which fell from 165.628 to 97.668 as a fear premium came out of the price.

Silver fell 7.85% over the week to 50.03, more than twice gold's drop. When silver falls much harder than gold, it usually means speculative, leveraged money was leaving precious metals, not that central banks or long-term holders changed their minds. Both metals bounced on 2 November: gold rose 1.31% and silver 1.9%.

For US bonds, the 2-year yield of 4.56% sits above the Fed funds upper limit of 4.0% and the effective rate of 3.88%. Read plainly, the bond market is not pricing a run of Fed cuts. The 10-year at 4.94% also leaves a high real yield of 2.60%. That is a costly backdrop for an asset like gold that pays no interest, and it caps how far gold can rise on rate hopes alone.

The dollar is not the problem for gold right now. The broad index was 121.6656 and barely moved on the day, and EUR/USD was steady at 1.1163. A clear dollar move after the midterms would be a new force rather than a continuation of one.

Official buying, the slow-moving floor under gold, is easing. IMF-reporting central banks bought a net 34.66 tonnes in September, down from 45.76 tonnes in August. They are still buying, but less, so dips have a little less official support.

watch.what_to_watch: Which party controls the House and the Senate. Then check how the 10-year real yield (now 2.60%) and the broad dollar (now 121.6656) react over the following days, rather than gold's first-hour move. A split Congress usually means less new fiscal spending, which would lean real yields lower and help gold modestly. A result that points to larger deficits could push long yields up from 4.94% and weigh on gold. The snapshot's only market hints are combination bets that bundle a Democratic Senate with unrelated events (Polymarket at 43.0%, Kalshi at 29.0%), so they cannot isolate the US outcome. Also check whether the Geopolitical Risk index keeps rising from 97.668, since that, not the election, drove last week.

risks.text: The geopolitical premium can swing back fast in either direction. The index jumped from 77.638 to 97.668 in a single day after falling from 165.628. Gold's next weekly move may track this index more than anything in Washington.

Real yields may stop falling. If the midterm result or the 9 December FOMC projections confirm that rates stay near current levels (2-year at 4.56% against a 4.0% upper limit), the 2.60% real yield would keep holding gold back. A hawkish signal at that meeting would cut against gold.

Selling by speculative holders may not be finished. Silver's 7.85% weekly fall shows leveraged money leaving, and slower central-bank buying (34.66 tonnes in September, down from 45.76 in August) offers a thinner cushion if that selling resumes.

Volatility is rising. The VIX rose 2.22 points to 19.42, and emerging-market stress is visible: the Brazilian real fell 7.61% over the week. In a dash for cash, gold can be sold to cover losses elsewhere before it acts as a safe haven.

consensus.view: There is no survey of gold forecasts in the snapshot, so 'consensus' here means models and market prices. The frozen gold-events model expects a small rebound over five days: gold +0.47% and silver +1.02%. It has been scored on 0 weeks out of sample, so it is untested. Bond pricing is the firmer signal. The 2-year at 4.56% above the 4.0% Fed upper limit implies no near-term easing cycle, while the 10-year real yield edged down to 2.60%. The market treats today's midterms and the 9 December FOMC as the next catalysts, and the bounce of 1.31% on 2 November suggests buyers see last week's 3.06% fall as overdone.

GOLD.might_be_wrong: The shared assumption is that gold trades off US real yields, the dollar and the Fed, so the midterms and the FOMC are what matter. Last week contradicts that. Real yields fell 6bp and the dollar rose only 0.28%, yet gold fell 3.06% and silver 7.85%, while the Geopolitical Risk index nearly halved from 165.628. If the fear premium and speculative positioning are now the main drivers, the midterm reaction could be smaller than people expect, and the next big move could come from a geopolitical headline instead. The model's +0.47% call is built on last week's changes in those same drivers and has no out-of-sample record, so it is no tiebreaker. My confidence is low to moderate. The most likely way I am wrong is a clear midterm result that moves the 10-year real yield sharply, putting the rates channel back in charge.
